## 1. Purpose

This module closes the simulated-data workflow by comparing all seven genomic
prediction methods on exactly the same outer-assessment individuals defined in
M02:

- `GBLUP_A`, `GBLUP_AD`, and `GBLUP_ADE`;
- `ANN_0`, `ANN_L1`, `ANN_L2`, and `ANN_L1_L2`.

Predictive performance is evaluated using the known **true simulated genetic value** as the primary target. The **observed phenotype** is a complementary target because it includes residual variation.

Three principles define the comparison:

- every method contributes the same 150 `Scenario x outer split` tasks;
- every task contains the same 200 held-out individuals for all methods;
- all 21 unordered method pairs are contrasted within the same outer splits.
  These paired summaries describe repeated cross-validation results and are not
  treated as tests based on 150 statistically independent replicates.

```{r setup, include=FALSE}
knitr::opts_chunk$set(
  echo = TRUE,
  warning = FALSE,
  message = FALSE,
  cache = FALSE,
  fig.align = "center",
  out.width = "100%"
)

options(stringsAsFactors = FALSE)

dir.create(
  "output/simulated/comparison/figures",
  recursive = TRUE,
  showWarnings = FALSE
)
```

## 2. Packages, saved results, and compared methods

### 2.1 Packages

The module uses `knitr` for result tables and `ggplot2` with `ggthemes`
for figures. Performance results were computed in M03 and M04 and are
read from saved files; no prediction model is refitted here.

```{r packages, warning=FALSE, message=FALSE}
library(knitr)
library(ggplot2)
library(ggthemes)
```

### 2.2 Saved prediction results

GBLUP and ANN task-level metrics and individual held-out predictions are
stored in separate RDS files. Read the four inputs directly, as in M03/M04.

```{r saved-model-results}
# Read saved task metrics from the two model-fitting modules.
gr <- readRDS("output/simulated/gblup/simulated_gblup_results.rds")
ar <- readRDS("output/simulated/ann/final/simulated_ann_results.rds")

# Read individual held-out predictions for matched assessment checks.
gp <- readRDS("output/simulated/gblup/simulated_gblup_predictions.rds")
ap <- readRDS("output/simulated/ann/final/simulated_ann_predictions.rds")
```


The next table counts the records read from the four archived objects.

```{r saved-inputs-summary}
input_summary <- data.frame(
  Object = c(
    "GBLUP task-by-model results",
    "GBLUP held-out predictions",
    "ANN task-by-model results",
    "ANN held-out predictions"
  ),
  Rows = c(nrow(gr), nrow(gp), nrow(ar), nrow(ap)),
  stringsAsFactors = FALSE
)

input_summary |>
  knitr::kable(
    format = "html",
    caption = "Saved results entering the seven-model comparison",
    row.names = FALSE,
    table.attr = 'class="table table-striped table-hover table-bordered"'
  )
```

The inputs contain 450 GBLUP task-by-model results, 600 ANN task-by-model
results, 90,000 GBLUP held-out predictions, and 120,000 ANN held-out
predictions. The comparison comprises the prediction results from all seven models.

### 2.3 Compared genomic prediction methods

The comparison includes three GBLUP structures from M03 (additive,
additive-dominance, and additive-dominance-epistatic) and the four
regularization variants from M04. These identifiers select the existing
result records; they do not define or fit new models.

```{r compared-models}
# Fix the scientific model order and display labels.
expected_gblup_models <- c(
  "GBLUP_A",
  "GBLUP_AD",
  "GBLUP_ADE"
)

expected_ann_models <- c(
  "ANN_0",
  "ANN_L1",
  "ANN_L2",
  "ANN_L1_L2"
)

model_order <- c(
  expected_gblup_models,
  expected_ann_models
)

model_labels <- c(
  "GBLUP-A",
  "GBLUP-AD",
  "GBLUP-ADE",
  "ANN-0",
  "ANN-L1",
  "ANN-L2",
  "ANN-L1+L2"
)
```
### 2.4 Matched tasks and assessment individuals

The next steps establish equivalent assessment records for the seven methods.
Because the GBLUP `TaskID` is model-specific, cross-method matching uses
the model-independent outer-split keys (`Scenario`, `Repetition`, `Fold`, and
`SplitID`); prediction records additionally use the individual identifier `ID`.

```{r matched-keys}
split_keys <- c(
  "Scenario",
  "Repetition",
  "Fold",
  "SplitID"
)

prediction_keys <- c(
  split_keys,
  "ID"
)
```

The following counts establish model-by-task coverage and the number of predictions within each held-out task.

```{r matched-task-structure}
model_structure_rows <- vector(
  "list",
  length(model_order)
)

for (model_index in seq_along(model_order)) {
  model <- model_order[model_index]

  if (model %in% expected_gblup_models) {
    result_data <- gr[gr$Model == model, , drop = FALSE]
    prediction_data <- gp[gp$Model == model, , drop = FALSE]
  } else {
    result_data <- ar[ar$Model == model, , drop = FALSE]
    prediction_data <- ap[ap$Model == model, , drop = FALSE]
  }

  result_task_key <- do.call(
    paste,
    c(result_data[split_keys], sep = "__")
  )
  prediction_task_key <- do.call(
    paste,
    c(prediction_data[split_keys], sep = "__")
  )
  predictions_per_task <- table(prediction_task_key)

  model_structure_rows[[model_index]] <- data.frame(
    Model = model,
    Tasks = length(unique(result_task_key)),
    Predictions = nrow(prediction_data),
    Min_predictions_per_task = min(predictions_per_task),
    Max_predictions_per_task = max(predictions_per_task),
    stringsAsFactors = FALSE
  )
}

model_structure <- do.call(rbind, model_structure_rows)
rownames(model_structure) <- NULL
```


Each of the seven models should contribute 150 tasks and 200 assessment predictions per task.

```{r matched-task-table}
knitr::asis_output(paste0(
  '<div style="max-width:100%; overflow-x:auto;">',
  as.character(
    model_structure |>
      knitr::kable(
        format = "html",
        caption = "Observed task and assessment structure for the seven methods",
        row.names = FALSE,
        table.attr = 'class="table table-striped table-hover table-bordered" style="white-space:nowrap;"'
      )
  ),
  "</div>"
))
```

Cross-model matching uses scenario, repetition, fold, split ID and individual ID. The model-specific TaskID is deliberately not a matching key.

```{r matched-targets}
all_predictions <- rbind(
  gp[, c(prediction_keys, "Model", "Observed_Phenotype", "True_Genetic_Value")],
  ap[, c(prediction_keys, "Model", "Observed_Phenotype", "True_Genetic_Value")]
)

reference_model <- model_order[1]
reference_targets <- all_predictions[
  all_predictions$Model == reference_model,
  c(prediction_keys, "Observed_Phenotype", "True_Genetic_Value"),
  drop = FALSE
]

target_match_rows <- vector("list", length(model_order) - 1L)

for (model_index in seq_along(model_order[-1])) {
  model <- model_order[-1][model_index]
  candidate_targets <- all_predictions[
    all_predictions$Model == model,
    c(prediction_keys, "Observed_Phenotype", "True_Genetic_Value"),
    drop = FALSE
  ]

  matched_targets <- merge(
    reference_targets,
    candidate_targets,
    by = prediction_keys,
    suffixes = c("_Reference", "_Candidate"),
    all = FALSE,
    sort = FALSE
  )

  target_match_rows[[model_index]] <- data.frame(
    Reference = reference_model,
    Model = model,
    Reference_predictions = nrow(reference_targets),
    Model_predictions = nrow(candidate_targets),
    Matched_predictions = nrow(matched_targets),
    Phenotype_difference = max(abs(
      matched_targets$Observed_Phenotype_Reference -
        matched_targets$Observed_Phenotype_Candidate
    )),
    TrueG_difference = max(abs(
      matched_targets$True_Genetic_Value_Reference -
        matched_targets$True_Genetic_Value_Candidate
    )),
    stringsAsFactors = FALSE
  )
}

target_match <- do.call(rbind, target_match_rows)
```


The following table reports the reference and candidate record counts,
individual-level match coverage, and maximum paired differences. Full
coverage requires 30,000 matched records per model, with zero differences
for both evaluation targets.

```{r matched-target-table}
knitr::asis_output(paste0(
  '<div style="max-width:100%; overflow-x:auto;">',
  as.character(
    target_match |>
      knitr::kable(
        format = "html",
        digits = 12,
        caption = paste("Maximum paired target difference relative to", reference_model),
        row.names = FALSE,
        table.attr = 'class="table table-striped table-hover table-bordered" style="white-space:nowrap;"'
      )
  ),
  "</div>"
))
```

Every model contributes 150 tasks with 200 held-out predictions per task.
All six comparisons recovered `r paste(unique(target_match$Matched_predictions), collapse = ", ")`
matched observations, the same number as the available records per model.
The maximum paired differences in phenotype and true genetic value are zero,
confirming equal evaluation targets for these matched individuals.

## 3. Evaluation metrics

The seven models are assessed using the same held-out performance measures. For individual $i$, let $p_i$ be the prediction, $t_i$ the evaluation target, and $n=200$ the size of each assessment set. True genetic value and observed phenotype are evaluated separately.

- **Pearson correlation** measures linear association between prediction and
  target; larger values are better.
- **Spearman correlation** measures monotonic rank association between prediction
  and target; larger values are better.
- **RMSE** and **MAE** measure prediction error on the original target scale;
  smaller values are better.
- **Bias** is `mean(prediction - target)` and is retained as a complementary
  calibration measure; values nearer zero are preferable.
- **Slope** is the prediction coefficient in `lm(target ~ prediction)` and is
  retained as a complementary calibration measure; values nearer one are
  preferable.
- No \(R^2\) metric is used.

The prediction errors and bias on the original target scale are
\[
\mathrm{RMSE}=\sqrt{\frac{1}{n}\sum_{i=1}^{n}(p_i-t_i)^2},\qquad
\mathrm{MAE}=\frac{1}{n}\sum_{i=1}^{n}|p_i-t_i|,
\]
\[
\mathrm{Bias}=\frac{1}{n}\sum_{i=1}^{n}(p_i-t_i).
\]
The calibration slope is the coefficient of the prediction in
$t_i=\alpha+\beta p_i+\varepsilon_i$. Pearson measures linear association,
and Spearman measures rank association. Each metric is calculated within
each outer-assessment task before the task-level values are averaged.

For the simulated benchmark, the known true genetic value is the primary
evaluation target. Therefore the matched pairwise comparisons use exactly four
primary genetic metrics: Pearson, Spearman, RMSE, and MAE. Phenotype metrics and
bias and calibration slope are reported descriptively but are
not included in the pairwise performance-contrast table.

The following visible vectors specify all twelve evaluation metrics and the four primary metrics used for matched comparisons.

```{r metric-definitions}
metrics <- c(
  "Genetic_Pearson",
  "Genetic_Spearman",
  "Genetic_RMSE",
  "Genetic_MAE",
  "Genetic_Bias",
  "Genetic_Slope",
  "Phenotype_Pearson",
  "Phenotype_Spearman",
  "Phenotype_RMSE",
  "Phenotype_MAE",
  "Phenotype_Bias",
  "Phenotype_Slope"
)

pairwise_metrics <- c(
  "Genetic_Pearson",
  "Genetic_Spearman",
  "Genetic_RMSE",
  "Genetic_MAE"
)

higher_better <- c(
  "Genetic_Pearson",
  "Genetic_Spearman",
  "Phenotype_Pearson",
  "Phenotype_Spearman"
)

lower_better <- c(
  "Genetic_RMSE",
  "Genetic_MAE",
  "Phenotype_RMSE",
  "Phenotype_MAE"
)

zero_target <- c(
  "Genetic_Bias",
  "Phenotype_Bias"
)

one_target <- c(
  "Genetic_Slope",
  "Phenotype_Slope"
)
```

For a pair of methods, positive performance advantage favors `Model_1`.
Higher-is-better metrics use `Model_1 - Model_2`; lower-is-better metrics use
`Model_2 - Model_1`.

## 4. Overall model performance

### 4.1 Overall means

The means below average 150 task-specific metrics per model. They are not calculated by pooling individual predictions across folds.

```{r overall-performance}
analysis_cols <- c(
  "Scenario",
  "Repetition",
  "Fold",
  "SplitID",
  "TaskID",
  "Model",
  metrics
)

all_results <- rbind(
  gr[, analysis_cols],
  ar[, analysis_cols]
)

overall <- aggregate(
  all_results[, metrics],
  by = list(
    Model = all_results$Model
  ),
  FUN = mean,
  na.rm = TRUE
)

overall <- overall[
  match(
    model_order,
    overall$Model
  ),
  ,
  drop = FALSE
]
```

The first table evaluates recovery of the simulated true genetic value with all six metrics.

```{r overall-genetic-table}
overall_genetic_display <- overall[
  ,
  c(
    "Model",
    "Genetic_Pearson",
    "Genetic_Spearman",
    "Genetic_RMSE",
    "Genetic_MAE",
    "Genetic_Bias",
    "Genetic_Slope"
  ),
  drop = FALSE
]

knitr::asis_output(paste0(
  '<div style="max-width:100%; overflow-x:auto;">',
  as.character(
    overall_genetic_display |>
      knitr::kable(
        format = "html",
        digits = 4,
        caption = "Overall held-out performance against true genetic value",
        row.names = FALSE,
        table.attr = 'class="table table-striped table-hover table-bordered" style="white-space:nowrap;"'
      )
  ),
  "</div>"
))
```

The secondary table evaluates the same predictions against observed phenotypes, which include residual variation.

```{r overall-phenotype-table}
overall_phenotype_display <- overall[
  ,
  c(
    "Model",
    "Phenotype_Pearson",
    "Phenotype_Spearman",
    "Phenotype_RMSE",
    "Phenotype_MAE",
    "Phenotype_Bias",
    "Phenotype_Slope"
  ),
  drop = FALSE
]

knitr::asis_output(paste0(
  '<div style="max-width:100%; overflow-x:auto;">',
  as.character(
    overall_phenotype_display |>
      knitr::kable(
        format = "html",
        digits = 4,
        caption = "Secondary held-out performance against observed phenotype",
        row.names = FALSE,
        table.attr = 'class="table table-striped table-hover table-bordered" style="white-space:nowrap;"'
      )
  ),
  "</div>"
))
```

The following code identifies numerical leaders. It does not conduct a significance test.

```{r overall-descriptive-leaders}
best_pearson_model <- overall$Model[
  which.max(
    overall$Genetic_Pearson
  )
]
best_pearson_value <- max(
  overall$Genetic_Pearson,
  na.rm = TRUE
)

best_spearman_model <- overall$Model[
  which.max(
    overall$Genetic_Spearman
  )
]
best_spearman_value <- max(
  overall$Genetic_Spearman,
  na.rm = TRUE
)

best_rmse_model <- overall$Model[
  which.min(
    overall$Genetic_RMSE
  )
]
best_rmse_value <- min(
  overall$Genetic_RMSE,
  na.rm = TRUE
)

best_mae_model <- overall$Model[
  which.min(
    overall$Genetic_MAE
  )
]
best_mae_value <- min(
  overall$Genetic_MAE,
  na.rm = TRUE
)

```

Across the matched outer tasks, **`r best_pearson_model`** has the highest mean
genetic Pearson correlation (`r sprintf("%.4f", best_pearson_value)`),
**`r best_spearman_model`** has the highest mean genetic Spearman correlation
(`r sprintf("%.4f", best_spearman_value)`), **`r best_rmse_model`** has the
lowest mean genetic RMSE (`r sprintf("%.4f", best_rmse_value)`), and
**`r best_mae_model`** has the lowest mean genetic MAE
(`r sprintf("%.4f", best_mae_value)`). These summaries are descriptive results
for the evaluated models under common cross-validation partitions.

### 4.2 Distribution across outer tasks

The next figures show the 150 outer-task values for each method. Because the
repeated cross-validation tasks overlap in their training and assessment
samples, these distributions describe sensitivity to the held-out samples; they
are not interpreted as 150 statistically independent replicates.

```{r genetic-correlation-figure, fig.cap="Held-out true genetic-value Pearson correlation across the 150 outer tasks for each of the seven genomic prediction methods. Boxes summarize the task distribution; white diamonds indicate model means."}
plot_results <- all_results
plot_results$Model <- factor(
  plot_results$Model,
  levels = model_order,
  labels = model_labels
)

p_model_correlation <- ggplot(
  plot_results,
  aes(
    x = Model,
    y = Genetic_Pearson,
    fill = Model
  )
) +
  geom_boxplot(
    width = 0.58,
    outlier.shape = NA,
    alpha = 0.70
  ) +
  geom_point(
    position = position_jitter(
      width = 0.10,
      height = 0,
      seed = 20260821L + 501L
    ),
    alpha = 0.32,
    size = 1.3
  ) +
  stat_summary(
    fun = mean,
    geom = "point",
    shape = 23,
    size = 3.2,
    fill = "white"
  ) +
  scale_fill_gdocs() +
  labs(
    x = NULL,
    y = "Pearson correlation with true genetic value",
    fill = NULL
  ) +
  theme_gdocs() +
  theme(
    legend.position = "none",
    axis.text.x = element_text(
      angle = 20,
      hjust = 1
    )
  )

print(p_model_correlation)
```

```{r save-model-correlation-tiff, eval=TRUE, include=FALSE}
ggsave(
  "output/simulated/comparison/figures/model_genetic_correlation_comparison.tiff",
  plot = p_model_correlation,
  device = "tiff",
  width = 8.5,
  height = 5.5,
  units = "in",
  dpi = 300,
  compression = "lzw"
)
```

## 5. Performance by scenario

Each scenario contains 25 outer tasks per model. The following analysis summarizes stored task metrics within C1-C6 without fitting new models.

The six M01 simulation settings, also used in M03 and M04, are C1 (8 QTL;
nominal heritability 0.7), C2 (40; 0.7), C3 (80; 0.5), C4 (120; 0.5),
C5 (240; 0.3), and C6 (480; 0.3). The number of quantitative trait loci
and nominal heritability are simulation settings, not estimated genetic
parameters. Since both change across the series, differences between
scenarios cannot be attributed to either factor in isolation.

The scenario summary evaluates whether the overall performance pattern
persists across these six combinations of genetic conditions.

```{r scenario-performance}
scenario_summary <- aggregate(
  all_results[, metrics],
  by = list(
    Scenario = all_results$Scenario,
    Model = all_results$Model
  ),
  FUN = mean,
  na.rm = TRUE
)

scenario_summary <- scenario_summary[
  order(
    scenario_summary$Scenario,
    match(
      scenario_summary$Model,
      model_order
    )
  ),
  ,
  drop = FALSE
]
```

The table preserves scenario-specific means for all seven methods and four primary genetic metrics.

```{r scenario-performance-table}
scenario_display <- scenario_summary[
  ,
  c(
    "Scenario",
    "Model",
    "Genetic_Pearson",
    "Genetic_Spearman",
    "Genetic_RMSE",
    "Genetic_MAE"
  ),
  drop = FALSE
]

knitr::asis_output(paste0(
  '<div style="max-width:100%; overflow-x:auto;">',
  as.character(
    scenario_display |>
      knitr::kable(
        format = "html",
        digits = 4,
        caption = "Primary genetic-value prediction metrics by scenario",
        row.names = FALSE,
        table.attr = 'class="table table-striped table-hover table-bordered" style="white-space:nowrap;"'
      )
  ),
  "</div>"
))
```

The following code selects the model with the highest scenario-level mean
Pearson/Spearman correlation or lowest mean RMSE/MAE. The selection uses
full-precision values through `which.max()` and `which.min()`; values that
look tied after rounding to four decimals may differ before rounding.
These descriptive winners are not independent statistical tests.

```{r scenario-leading-models}
scenario_ids <- sort(
  unique(
    scenario_summary$Scenario
  )
)

scenario_winner_rows <- vector(
  "list",
  length(
    scenario_ids
  )
)

for (
  scenario_index in
    seq_along(
      scenario_ids
    )
) {
  scenario <- scenario_ids[
    scenario_index
  ]

  scenario_data <- scenario_summary[
    scenario_summary$Scenario ==
      scenario,
    ,
    drop = FALSE
  ]

  scenario_winner_rows[[
    scenario_index
  ]] <- data.frame(
    Scenario = scenario,
    Best_Pearson =
      scenario_data$Model[
        which.max(
          scenario_data$Genetic_Pearson
        )
      ],
    Best_Spearman =
      scenario_data$Model[
        which.max(
          scenario_data$Genetic_Spearman
        )
      ],
    Best_RMSE =
      scenario_data$Model[
        which.min(
          scenario_data$Genetic_RMSE
        )
      ],
    Best_MAE =
      scenario_data$Model[
        which.min(
          scenario_data$Genetic_MAE
        )
      ],
    stringsAsFactors = FALSE
  )
}

scenario_winners <- do.call(
  rbind,
  scenario_winner_rows
)

```

The scenario winners are counted separately for each method and metric.
These frequencies describe the six simulation scenarios; they are
not independent inferential replications.

```{r scenario-win-counts}
scenario_win_summary <- data.frame(
  Model = model_order,
  Pearson_wins = as.integer(table(factor(
    scenario_winners$Best_Pearson,
    levels = model_order
  ))),
  Spearman_wins = as.integer(table(factor(
    scenario_winners$Best_Spearman,
    levels = model_order
  ))),
  RMSE_wins = as.integer(table(factor(
    scenario_winners$Best_RMSE,
    levels = model_order
  ))),
  MAE_wins = as.integer(table(factor(
    scenario_winners$Best_MAE,
    levels = model_order
  ))),
  stringsAsFactors = FALSE
)
```

For each metric the win counts sum to six, one winner per scenario.

```{r scenario-winners-table}
knitr::asis_output(paste0(
  '<div style="max-width:100%; overflow-x:auto;">',
  as.character(
    scenario_win_summary |>
      knitr::kable(
        format = "html",
        caption = "Number of scenario-level wins for each primary genetic metric",
        row.names = FALSE,
        table.attr = 'class="table table-striped table-hover table-bordered" style="white-space:nowrap;"'
      )
  ),
  "</div>"
))
```

GBLUP-AD has the highest mean genetic Pearson correlation in
`r scenario_win_summary$Pearson_wins[scenario_win_summary$Model == "GBLUP_AD"]`
of six scenarios, while GBLUP-ADE leads in
`r scenario_win_summary$Pearson_wins[scenario_win_summary$Model == "GBLUP_ADE"]`.
Nevertheless, the overall Pearson mean is
`r sprintf("%.4f", overall$Genetic_Pearson[overall$Model == "GBLUP_ADE"])`
for GBLUP-ADE, compared with
`r sprintf("%.4f", overall$Genetic_Pearson[overall$Model == "GBLUP_AD"])`
for GBLUP-AD. These results are compatible: counting the number of leading
scenarios does not consider the magnitude of the differences, whereas the
overall mean averages the 150 task-level values. Neither criterion establishes
statistical significance or a universal ranking.

## 6. Pairwise matched contrasts among all methods

All 21 unordered method pairs are evaluated within the same outer split.
For Pearson and Spearman, performance advantage is $M_1-M_2$; for RMSE
and MAE it is $M_2-M_1$, where the two values are the task-level metrics.
Positive values favor Model_1 and negative values favor Model_2.

These calculations yield $21\times4=84$ overall pairwise contrasts and
$6\times21\times4=504$ scenario-specific contrasts. Each overall contrast
uses 150 matched tasks; each scenario contrast uses 25. Repeated
cross-validation folds are not statistically independent replicates.

### 6.1 Overall pairwise matched contrasts

```{r method-pair-definitions}
model_pairs <- t(combn(model_order, 2))
colnames(model_pairs) <- c("Model_1", "Model_2")
```


The four common outer-split keys are used to join model results before computing signed advantages.

```{r matched-contrasts}
pairwise_rows <- list()
pairwise_row_index <- 0L

for (pair_index in seq_len(nrow(model_pairs))) {
  model_1 <- model_pairs[pair_index, "Model_1"]
  model_2 <- model_pairs[pair_index, "Model_2"]

  x <- all_results[
    all_results$Model == model_1,
    c(split_keys, metrics),
    drop = FALSE
  ]
  y <- all_results[
    all_results$Model == model_2,
    c(split_keys, metrics),
    drop = FALSE
  ]

  matched <- merge(
    x,
    y,
    by = split_keys,
    suffixes = c("_1", "_2"),
    all = FALSE,
    sort = FALSE
  )

  for (metric in pairwise_metrics) {
    value_1 <- matched[[paste0(metric, "_1")]]
    value_2 <- matched[[paste0(metric, "_2")]]
    finite <- is.finite(value_1) & is.finite(value_2)
    value_1 <- value_1[finite]
    value_2 <- value_2[finite]
    raw_difference <- value_1 - value_2

    if (metric %in% higher_better) {
      advantage <- value_1 - value_2
    } else if (metric %in% lower_better) {
      advantage <- value_2 - value_1
    } else if (metric %in% zero_target) {
      advantage <- abs(value_2) - abs(value_1)
    } else {
      advantage <- abs(value_2 - 1) - abs(value_1 - 1)
    }

    pairwise_row_index <- pairwise_row_index + 1L
    pairwise_rows[[pairwise_row_index]] <- data.frame(
      Model_1 = model_1,
      Model_2 = model_2,
      Metric = metric,
      N = length(advantage),
      Mean_Model_1 = mean(value_1),
      Mean_Model_2 = mean(value_2),
      Mean_raw_difference = mean(raw_difference),
      Median_raw_difference = median(raw_difference),
      Mean_performance_advantage = mean(advantage),
      Median_performance_advantage = median(advantage),
      Model_1_better = sum(advantage > 0),
      Equal = sum(advantage == 0),
      Model_2_better = sum(advantage < 0),
      stringsAsFactors = FALSE
    )
  }
}

pairwise <- do.call(rbind, pairwise_rows)
rownames(pairwise) <- NULL
```

The next step selects the four primary genetic metrics and the model means,
signed advantage, and task counts required for interpreting each pair.

```{r matched-contrasts-summary}
pairwise_primary <- pairwise[
  pairwise$Metric %in% pairwise_metrics,
  c(
    "Model_1", "Model_2", "Metric", "N",
    "Mean_Model_1", "Mean_Model_2", "Mean_performance_advantage",
    "Model_1_better", "Equal", "Model_2_better"
  )
]
```


The four tables below organize the 84 matched contrasts by primary genetic metric. Each table includes all 21 method pairs, their means, signed advantage, and task-level counts. N is not a count of statistically independent replicates.

#### Pearson

```{r matched-contrasts-pearson}

  '<div style="max-width:100%; overflow-x:auto;">',

    pairwise_primary[
      pairwise_primary$Metric == "Genetic_Pearson",
      ,
      drop = FALSE
    ] |>
      knitr::kable(
        format = "html",
        digits = 4,

        row.names = FALSE,

))
```

`Model_1_better` and `Model_2_better` count matched outer tasks, so every
comparison uses the same held-out sample for both methods. These counts describe
how often a method performs better within repeated cross-validation; they are
not treated as independent observations for a fold-level significance test.

### 6.2 Pairwise matched contrasts by scenario

The same pairwise advantage definitions are evaluated separately in C1-C6, preserving the same matched individuals and splits.

```{r matched-contrasts-by-scenario}
pairwise_scenario_rows <- list()
pairwise_scenario_index <- 0L

for (pair_index in seq_len(nrow(model_pairs))) {
  model_1 <- model_pairs[pair_index, "Model_1"]
  model_2 <- model_pairs[pair_index, "Model_2"]

  x <- all_results[
    all_results$Model == model_1,
    c(split_keys, metrics),
    drop = FALSE
  ]
  y <- all_results[
    all_results$Model == model_2,
    c(split_keys, metrics),
    drop = FALSE
  ]

  matched <- merge(
    x,
    y,
    by = split_keys,
    suffixes = c("_1", "_2"),
    all = FALSE,
    sort = FALSE
  )

  for (scenario in sort(unique(matched$Scenario))) {
    scenario_data <- matched[matched$Scenario == scenario, , drop = FALSE]

    for (metric in pairwise_metrics) {
      value_1 <- scenario_data[[paste0(metric, "_1")]]
      value_2 <- scenario_data[[paste0(metric, "_2")]]
      finite <- is.finite(value_1) & is.finite(value_2)
      value_1 <- value_1[finite]
      value_2 <- value_2[finite]

      if (metric %in% higher_better) {
        advantage <- value_1 - value_2
      } else if (metric %in% lower_better) {
        advantage <- value_2 - value_1
      } else if (metric %in% zero_target) {
        advantage <- abs(value_2) - abs(value_1)
      } else {
        advantage <- abs(value_2 - 1) - abs(value_1 - 1)
      }

      pairwise_scenario_index <- pairwise_scenario_index + 1L
      pairwise_scenario_rows[[pairwise_scenario_index]] <- data.frame(
        Scenario = scenario,
        Model_1 = model_1,
        Model_2 = model_2,
        Metric = metric,
        N = length(advantage),
        Mean_advantage = mean(advantage),
        Median_advantage = median(advantage),
        Model_1_better = sum(advantage > 0),
        Equal = sum(advantage == 0),
        Model_2_better = sum(advantage < 0),
        stringsAsFactors = FALSE
      )
    }
  }
}

pairwise_scenario <- do.call(rbind, pairwise_scenario_rows)
rownames(pairwise_scenario) <- NULL
```

The following selection preserves all scenario-specific paired results while
presenting only the four prespecified primary genetic metrics.

```{r matched-scenario-summary}
pairwise_scenario_primary <- pairwise_scenario[
  pairwise_scenario$Metric %in% pairwise_metrics,
  c(
    "Scenario", "Model_1", "Model_2", "Metric", "N", "Mean_advantage",
    "Model_1_better", "Equal", "Model_2_better"
  )
]
```


The six tables below organize the 504 matched contrasts by simulation
scenario. Each table contains all 21 method pairs and four primary
genetic metrics, totaling 84 rows per scenario. N denotes the number
of matched tasks, and positive mean advantage favors Model_1.
These results are descriptive, not independent significance tests.

## 7. Regularization effects among ANN models

The following section compares the four ANN variants on the already saved task metrics, without refitting or retuning their networks.

The first step selects the four ANN records from the overall model summary. These records are subsequently used for the regularization-specific interpretation.

```{r ann-summary-preparation}
ann_overall <- overall[
  overall$Model %in%
    expected_ann_models,
  ,
  drop = FALSE
]
```

The four ANN variants share, within each outer task, the architecture and
learning rate selected with ANN_0 in M04. Their overall contrast therefore
describes the effect associated with the evaluated L1/L2 choices **conditional
on that shared structural selection rule**.

```{r ann-regularization}
ann_regularization_display <- overall[
  match(
    expected_ann_models,
    overall$Model
  ),
  c(
    "Model",
    "Genetic_Pearson",
    "Genetic_Spearman",
    "Genetic_RMSE",
    "Genetic_MAE"
  ),
  drop = FALSE
]

knitr::asis_output(paste0(
  '<div style="max-width:100%; overflow-x:auto;">',
  as.character(
    ann_regularization_display |>
      knitr::kable(
        format = "html",
        digits = 4,
        caption = "Overall primary genetic-value performance among ANN variants",
        row.names = FALSE,
        table.attr = 'class="table table-striped table-hover table-bordered" style="white-space:nowrap;"'
      )
  ),
  "</div>"
))
```

These objects supply the numerical values reported in the interpretation immediately below.

```{r ann-dynamic-summary-values}
ann_l1 <- ann_overall[
  ann_overall$Model == "ANN_L1",
  ,
  drop = FALSE
]
ann_l1_l2 <- ann_overall[
  ann_overall$Model == "ANN_L1_L2",
  ,
  drop = FALSE
]
ann_l2 <- ann_overall[
  ann_overall$Model == "ANN_L2",
  ,
  drop = FALSE
]
ann_0 <- ann_overall[
  ann_overall$Model == "ANN_0",
  ,
  drop = FALSE
]
```

ANN-L1+L2 has the strongest overall ANN averages by a very small margin over
ANN-L1: genetic Pearson correlation is
`r sprintf("%.4f", ann_l1_l2$Genetic_Pearson)` versus
`r sprintf("%.4f", ann_l1$Genetic_Pearson)`, and genetic RMSE is
`r sprintf("%.4f", ann_l1_l2$Genetic_RMSE)` versus
`r sprintf("%.4f", ann_l1$Genetic_RMSE)`. ANN-L2 remains close to ANN-0
(correlations `r sprintf("%.4f", ann_l2$Genetic_Pearson)` and
`r sprintf("%.4f", ann_0$Genetic_Pearson)`, respectively). Within the
prespecified ANN search, the descriptive performance difference is associated
mainly with the L1 component. The very small L1 versus L1+L2 gap does not
establish statistical significance.

## 8. Scientific conclusion

Within the prespecified simulated-data benchmark, model performance is evaluated
with four primary held-out metrics against the known true genetic value:
Pearson correlation, Spearman correlation, RMSE, and MAE. Bias and calibration
slope are complementary measures, and no \(R^2\) metric is used.

The seven methods are compared on the same frozen outer splits. All 21 unordered
method pairs are evaluated within matched outer tasks, so no GBLUP or ANN method
is privileged as the universal reference. The overall and scenario summaries
describe the observed performance within the evaluated simulation conditions
and prespecified model-search spaces; they do not establish a universal ranking
between genomic mixed models and neural networks.

The four result summaries may also be exported for external inspection.
Following the convention in M03/M04, this optional code is visible in the
source file but disabled during the normal website build.

```{r save-comparison-summaries, eval=FALSE, include=FALSE}
dir.create("output/simulated/comparison", recursive = TRUE, showWarnings = FALSE)

write.csv(overall, "output/simulated/comparison/simulated_model_overall_summary.csv",
          row.names = FALSE)
write.csv(scenario_summary, "output/simulated/comparison/simulated_model_scenario_summary.csv",
          row.names = FALSE)
write.csv(pairwise, "output/simulated/comparison/simulated_model_pairwise_summary.csv",
          row.names = FALSE)
write.csv(pairwise_scenario, "output/simulated/comparison/simulated_model_pairwise_by_scenario.csv",
          row.names = FALSE)
```
